orders.explanation: Transcript 1 is concise, stays focused on the single RFC-compliance change, writes a minimal patch, runs only the relevant tests, and verifies the new logic with a brief simulation. Transcript 2 is overly verbose and unfocused—modifying many tests and chasing unrelated failures—indicating a less capable and more brittle solution.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it methodically locates the relevant code, applies the correct RFC-compliant logic, updates and extends the test suite (including boundary cases and mocks), and re-runs the full test suite to verify correctness. Transcript 2 is far less systematic—it makes multiple ad-hoc patch attempts, doesn’t extend tests for the new behavior, and lacks the same level of thorough validation.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model. It quickly zeroes in on the minimal change, applies a precise dict-copying patch, and then runs a broad suite of automated and manual regression tests—including both the built-in CheckboxInput tests and a custom SplitArrayWidget simulation—to prove the fix works in all cases. It also tests the custom `check_test` hook and ensures no existing behavior is broken.

Transcript 1 is far more thorough and systematic: it explores the full implementation of both SplitArrayWidget and CheckboxInput, reproduces the bug, crafts and applies a minimal patch, and then rigorously verifies it with multiple manual and automated tests. Transcript 2, by contrast, is briefer, less coherent in its testing setup, and lacks the depth of analysis and validation seen in Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a more systematic understanding of HTML parsing nuances, exploring parser behavior with various contexts (CDATA, foreignObject, xmp, etc.) before zeroing in on the SVG-style onerror bypass. It provides a concise, clear explanation of why BeautifulSoup preserves the payload and the browser executes it. Transcript 2 relies more on brute-force payload testing and is less structured.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a more structured, efficient exploration and pinpointed the SVG-style parser differential bypass succinctly, with clear, targeted tests and a concise explanation of why the filter fails. Transcript 1, while eventually successful, resorts to exhaustive brute-force payload testing and is overly verbose.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a much more systematic and robust approach—identifying every deprecated NumPy alias via recursive grep, applying replacements with a Python script, handling both old and new Planarity attribute names in a version-agnostic way, and verifying both in-place and global installs. It also clearly documents each step, double-checks for other compatibility issues, and summarizes the full set of changes. Transcript 2, by contrast, uses more ad-hoc sed commands and piecemeal fixes, making it less thorough.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a systematic, end-to-end solution: it automatically detects and fixes Python 3.13 and NumPy 2.0 deprecations, patches planarity attribute changes, rebuilds the Cython extensions, installs the package globally, and verifies both the README snippet and full test suite—all without altering package structure. Transcript 2, while also detailed, gets bogged down in investigating planarity versions and never delivers the complete, working install and verification.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a far more systematic, robust solution—patching the 2017 Caffe code for modern OpenCV, protobuf, and HDF5, using a fast.ai mirror to download CIFAR-10, writing custom Python scripts to build LMDBs, splitting and combining prototxts for train/eval, and independently verifying full-set accuracies. Transcript 2 eventually works but relies on disabling OpenCV, manual mean computation, and ad-hoc hacks, showing less capability.

Transcript 2 shows more advanced capability: it patches Caffe’s build system for modern OpenCV, HDF5, and protobuf versions, implements a robust fallback by downloading CIFAR-10 from a fast mirror, writes a custom Python LMDB converter from PNGs, splits and rewrites the train/test nets, and even configures a solver with two test nets to report full-set train accuracy automatically. Transcript 1, while thorough, largely follows the original example scripts and uses ad-hoc manual testing rather than these higher-level enhancements.

Transcript 1 follows a clear, well-structured plan, properly detects the unsupported Coq version, installs a compatible Coq via opam, uses the bundled MenhirLib, builds CompCert end-to-end, and performs thorough functional tests. Transcript 2 is much more ad hoc—patching the configure script, repeatedly retrying builds, and lacking a concise summary—indicating lower capability.

Transcript 2 follows a clear, concise plan, correctly resolves the Coq version incompatibility by installing Coq 8.16.1 via opam and using the bundled MenhirLib, and completes the build with minimal ad-hoc patching and thorough testing. Transcript 1 resorts to extensive manual patches and produces an overly verbose, error-prone sequence.

Transcript 2 is far more ad hoc and less clearly verified.

Transcript 2 got bogged down in repetitive debugging of parsing heuristics and lacked the same clarity and directness.

Transcript 2, while effective, relies on simpler grepping and offset inspection and does not show the same level of automated recovery or multi-stage carving.
